stories.title: Data Center Giant Equinix Ups Its 2026 Forecast Behind Robust Q2
stories.excerpt: Equinix significantly increased its forecasts and expectations for 2026 after posting another record-heavy quarter on the back of artificial intelligence demand and more data center construction. The Redwood City, Calif.-based data center real estate investment trust (REIT) generated $2.63 billion in second-quarter revenue, up 7 percent from $2.44 billion in the first quarter and 16 percent from $2.26 billion a year earlier. Equinix said operating growth and one-time fees from the company’s xScale hyperscale business boosted its results. Net income reached $477 million, up from $415 million in the first quarter and $367 million during the second quarter of 2025. Net income attributable to common shareholders totaled $479 million, or $4.83 per share. Funds from operations (FFO), REITs’ main cashflow measure, rose to $854 million from $758 million in the previous quarter and $689 million a year earlier. Equinix delivered $424 million in annualized gross bookings, its highest second-quarter total and second-highest quarterly volume on record. Bookings increased from $378 million during the first quarter and $345 million in the second quarter of 2025. The company also generated approximately $110 million in presales. “The vast majority of our largest deals were driven by AI workloads,” CEO Adaire Fox-Martin said during the company’s Wednesday earnings call. She added that Equinix’s revised outlook “reflects a market opportunity that has materially improved over the past 12 months.” Stabilized data centers remained approximately 82 percent utilized, in line with the first quarter. The stabilized portfolio generated $1.89 billion in revenue, up 7 percent annually, while producing a 27 percent cash return on gross property investment, compared with 24 percent a year earlier. Equinix ended the quarter with 52 projects underway across 33 markets after adding nine since April, including new projects in Chicago and abroad. bullets: Equinix Q2 revenue $2.63B, up 16% YoY; raised 2026 guidance on AI/hyperscale demand
FFO rose to $854M from $689M YoY; xScale hyperscale business driving growth

stories.summary: Equinix posted record second-quarter revenue of $2.63 billion (up 16% YoY) and significantly raised 2026 forecasts, driven by artificial intelligence demand and hyperscale build-out. Net income reached $477 million and FFO climbed to $854 million, up 24% from the prior year. The company's xScale hyperscale business and one-time fees fueled the outperformance, with annualized gross bookings of $424 million marking the second-highest quarterly total.
stories.impact: Robust AI data center capex signals sustained commercial real estate and industrial demand across major metros, but more critically indicates a multi-year structural shift in tech employment and office consolidation toward smaller, specialized footprints in hubs like Austin, Phoenix, and Northern Virginia—affecting workforce composition and remote-work policy, which ripple into apartment demand patterns and submarket selectivity.

stories.title: U.S. Apartment Rents Post Eighth Consecutive Month of Growth
stories.excerpt: U.S. apartment rents were essentially flat in July, with the national average rising +0.03% to $1,747 from June’s upwardly revised level of $1,746, CoStar Group’s Apartments.com reported Wednesday. This marks the eighth consecutive month of positive rent increases following a period of flat to declining monthly performance in the second half of 2025. On an annual basis, rent growth accelerated to +1.0% in July 2026 from the upwardly revised +0.9% in June and was slightly down from the +1.1% reading recorded one year earlier. June 2026 was initially reported as a +0.1% month-over-month increase and has been revised upward to +0.2%. Although apartment rent growth typically slows as the market moves further into the summer leasing season, gains in July were particularly subdued. “Following modest rent increases during the spring, the +0.03% increase recorded in July represents a notable slowdown in monthly pricing momentum,” according to Apartments.com. “While annual rent growth continues to improve gradually, elevated supply levels continue to restrain pricing momentum nationally.” Where the apartment industry connects. Meet the owners, investors, developers, lenders, brokers, and service providers driving today’s multifamily market at Connect Apartments. bullets: National avg rent $1,747 in July; 8 consecutive months of positive growth post-soft 2025
Annual rent growth +1.0% in July, up from +0.9% in June but slightly below prior-year +1.1%
Elevated supply levels continue to restrain monthly pricing momentum despite consecutive monthly gains
stories.summary: U.S. apartment rents rose +0.03% month-over-month in July 2026 to $1,747, marking the eighth consecutive month of positive rent growth following soft pricing in late 2025. Annual rent growth accelerated modestly to +1.0% in July from +0.9% in June, though it trails the +1.1% rate recorded one year prior. CoStar flagged that elevated supply nationwide continues to cap pricing momentum even as monthly gains persist into the summer leasing season.
stories.impact: Sustained supply overhang is beginning to pressure rent growth acceleration nationally, signaling that new deliveries are outpacing absorption in key markets and absorption rates are slowing—a critical reality check for developers on market-by-market underwriting and the window for value-add repositioning deals (see Article 3) before cap rate compression cycles through and carry costs rise.

stories.title: Costa Mesa Multifamily Changes Hands for Value-Add Repositioning
stories.excerpt: Marcus & Millichap finalized the sale of 1990 Maple Ave., a 41-unit multifamily property in Costa Mesa. The property sold for $16.9 million or $412,195 per unit, approximately $550,000 above the property’s 2018 selling price. “Sundance West Apartment Homes presented a rare opportunity to acquire a low-density multifamily community in one of Orange County’s most supply-constrained rental markets,” said Matthew Kipp, senior managing director investments. “The property’s unique concentration of two- and three-bedroom floor plans and the meaningful capital improvements completed by prior ownership, including electrical upgrades and roof replacements, attracted significant investor interest. The competitive bidding environment allowed the seller to look beyond price alone and select a buyer whose local experience provided the highest confidence in execution.” Kipp and Tyler Leeson, executive managing director investments, in Marcus & Millichap’s Orange County office, marketed the property on behalf of the seller, a local family, exchanging out-of-state to reduce hands-on management, and procured the buyer, a professional investor acquiring for value-add repositioning. The post Costa Mesa Multifamily Changes Hands for Value-Add Repositioning appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Costa Mesa 41-unit property sold for $16.9M ($412K/unit), $550K above 2018 price
Buyer: professional investor acquiring for value-add repositioning in supply-constrained Orange County
Prior ownership completed electrical, roof upgrades; asset marketed on supply scarcity and 2–3-bed floor plans
stories.summary: Marcus & Millichap closed the sale of Sundance West Apartment Homes at 1990 Maple Ave. in Costa Mesa for $16.9 million ($412,195/unit), approximately $550,000 above its 2018 sale price. The low-density, 41-unit community—featuring mostly two- and three-bedroom units with recent capital improvements—attracted significant bidding from a professional investor targeting value-add repositioning. The broker emphasized Orange County's supply-constrained rental market as a draw.
stories.impact: Costa Mesa's supply constraints and small-building scarcity are sustaining pricing power and attracting value-add capital, but the modest unit count and density limit IRR potential—signaling that developers should focus on larger land parcels or assemblies in Orange County to achieve meaningful scale, particularly as supply constraints translate into sustained rent growth if absorption remains healthy.

stories.title: NYC Issues Partial Stop-Work Order at SL Green’s 750 Third Avenue Conversion
stories.excerpt: New York City’s Department of Buildings (DOB) has halted construction work at the third office-to-conversion project in Manhattan this month. The DOB issued a partial stop-work order at SL Green Realty’s $805 million conversion project at 750 Third Avenue in Midtown East, which is set to result in 680 residential units and potentially see 11 floors added. The halt comes after the near-collapse of the former Pfizer headquarters earlier in July, when steel beams at MetroLoft and David Werner’s 235 East 42nd Street project buckled and sparked the evacuation of 10 surrounding Midtown blocks. Earlier this week, GFP Real Estate’s conversion project at 222 Broadway in the Financial District was also halted after cracks were found on a newly added floor. In the case of 750 Third Avenue, it seems as if steel columns were not welded properly and inconsistencies were reported, according to the DOB. As a result, inspectors have temporarily stopped all steel work above the eighth floor at the 34-story property, according to The New York Times, which first reported the news. “During our structural reinforcement prep work, prior to beginning any overbuild work, we identified an on-site condition that differed from the plans that were submitted to the city, which was visible only after completing initial preparation work,” an SL Green spokesperson said in a statement to Commercial Observer. “There are no structural issues with the building, and we are already working with the licensed professional engineer of record to address this condition,” the spokesperson added. “We do not anticipate any impact to the overall project schedule, with other work ongoing, and have already submitted our request to rescind the partial stop work order.” While the Pfizer buckling certainly spurred a renewed scrutiny of ongoing conversion projects in New York City and an increased focus on safety, these types of partial stop-work orders are not uncommon. bullets: NYC DOB issued partial stop-work at SL Green's $805M 750 Third Ave conversion (680 units, +11 floors)
Third office-to-residential conversion halted in July; prior incidents: 235 East 42nd buckled steel; 222 Broadway cracks

stories.summary: New York City's Department of Buildings issued a partial stop-work order at SL Green Realty's $805 million office-to-residential conversion at 750 Third Avenue in Midtown East, which is planned to yield 680 units and add 11 floors. The halt follows two other Manhattan conversion stoppages in July—a steel beam collapse at MetroLoft's 235 East 42nd Street and cracks discovered at GFP Real Estate's 222 Broadway project. At 750 Third, inspectors found improperly welded steel columns and stopped all steel work above the eighth floor.
stories.impact: A cluster of structural failures across three major Manhattan office-to-residential conversions signals potential systemic quality-control and design-review breakdowns that will likely trigger enhanced city inspection protocols, longer permitting cycles, and higher construction contingencies—pushing total development costs up and timelines out across the NYC conversion pipeline, which may force smaller sponsors to abandon marginal deals and consolidate opportunity among better-capitalized firms.

Wharton Equity Partners renewed its 3,200-SF lease. The landlord is rolling out a prebuilt office program and planned cosmetic lobby renovations to support leasing momentum.
stories.impact: Steady leasing at mid-grade Midtown East office properties, buoyed by a new prebuilt program and light capex, indicates that trophy office is not the only segment capturing tenant demand—suggesting that developers and investors should consider selective repositioning of secondary/tertiary office assets rather than conversion in softer markets, as light modernization and flexible space can compete with conversions on time-to-lease and capital efficiency.

stories.title: BGO, Yukon Real Estate Partners Sell 291K-SF Kansas Cold Storage Facility
stories.excerpt: BGO and Yukon Real Estate Partners announced the sale of New Century Cold Storage, a newly built 291,000-square-foot, plant-attached, rail-served cold storage warehouse in New Century, Kansas, to a MetLife Investment Management client. The facility, owned and co-developed through a joint venture between BGO and Yukon, was purpose-built as a plant-attached, build-to-suit warehouse for CJ Logistics America. “With its purpose-built design, strategic location, and direct integration with food production and logistics operations, we believe this facility will make a meaningful contribution to the strength and resilience of U.S. food supply chains for decades to come,” said Kevin Rivest, Managing Partner, BGO. The New Century facility is located within the Johnson County Airport Commission’s New Century AirCenter industrial park, with a direct rail spur to the building and access to the BNSF Railway transcontinental intermodal facility. The property is positioned less than four miles from Interstate 35. The post BGO, Yukon Real Estate Partners Sell 291K-SF Kansas Cold Storage Facility appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: BGO and Yukon sold 291K-SF rail-served cold storage in New Century, Kansas to MetLife client

stories.summary: BGO and Yukon Real Estate Partners closed the sale of New Century Cold Storage, a newly built 291,000-square-foot plant-attached, rail-served cold storage warehouse in New Century, Kansas, to a MetLife Investment Management client. The facility was purpose-built as a build-to-suit warehouse for CJ Logistics America and is strategically sited within the New Century AirCenter industrial park, integrating directly with food production and logistics operations.
stories.impact: Cold storage and specialized logistics infrastructure are capturing institutional capital (MetLife) and generating strong demand in secondary/tertiary industrial markets—a signal that last-mile and food-supply-chain logistics are driving employment and population into secondary metros like Kansas City, which will underpin apartment demand in adjacent residential markets; developers should monitor CJ Logistics' footprint expansion for residential job-creation signals.

stories.title: AI Platform Clay Leases 44K SF with Swig Company
stories.excerpt: The Swig Company has leased 44,000 square feet at The Mills Building to artificial intelligence platform Clay. The lease was announced two weeks after Swig refinanced the circa-1891 property at 220 Montgomery St. in San Francisco’s Financial District. “The Mills Building continues to attract companies seeking a workplace that reflects their culture and ambitions,” said Stacia Keisner, SVP of asset management at The Swig Company. “Clay’s lease is another example of an innovative business choosing downtown San Francisco to recruit talent, foster collaboration, and position themselves for long-term success.” Cory Kristoff, EVP, director of leasing, added, “Through our focused spec suite initiative at the Mills Building, we have leased more than 102,000 square feet of space year to date, representing approximately 21% of the property. We are encouraged by this strong leasing momentum and expect it to continue throughout the remainder of the year and beyond.” Bart O’Connor, Mark Geisreiter and Hannah Potter of Newmark represented The Swig Company. stories.impact: AI companies are actively seeking downtown San Francisco office space at scale, signaling a reversal of tech-sector remote work and a re-concentration in major financial hubs—this employment influx will increase residential demand pressure in SF and Oakland submarkets, driving multifamily fundamentals and supporting conversion economics, but also intensifying competitive leasing for talent in an undersupplied residential market.

stories.title: City Selects Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies to Build 980 Homes in LIC
stories.excerpt: A development team made up of Slate Property Group, Hudson Companies and Volunteers of America has been chosen to create nearly 1,000 new homes upon a vacant parcel in Long Island City, Queens. The 70,000-square-foot development, at 54-42 Second Street, will be called the Orion, and two-thirds of its units will be set aside as affordable housing. “It is exactly what New York needs,” David Schwartz, principal and co-founder of Slate Property Group, said in a statement. “And we look forward to working with City Hall to get shovels in the ground as soon as possible.” The parcel sits within the 30-acre Hunter’s Point South housing complex. When completed, Hunter’s Point South is expected to feature approximately 5,000 new homes, roughly 3,000 of which will be affordable. The city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) began courting developers for the site, known as Parcel E, in June of last year. The request for proposals came with the requirement that Parcel E host more affordable homes than previous phases. The Orion will include approximately 980 new apartments. Two-thirds of the apartments, roughly 658 units, will be income-restricted, affordable to extremely low- to moderate-income households. Approximately 150 units will be set aside as supportive apartments. “Reaching households at every income level in a high-opportunity neighborhood like Hunter’s Point reflects a simple belief: Where New Yorkers live shouldn’t come down to income alone,” said Laszlo Syrop, principal and head of acquisitions at Hudson Companies. The mixed-use community, designed by Marvel Architects, will feature an affordable child care center, a workforce development center and a community pool. Approximately 6,000 square feet of ground-floor commercial retail space will also be made available along Second Street and Center Boulevard. The project, called The Orion at 54-42 Second Street, will occupy 70,000 square feet with roughly two-thirds of units (approximately 653) designated as affordable housing. stories.impact: The city's commitment to large-scale, publicly-led mixed-income development in LIC will lock in affordable housing production and moderate near-term market-rate rent upside in Queens waterfront submarkets, but the multi-year timeline to build-out and the density of affordability requirements will compress developer returns and capital stacks—limiting private market appetite for competing market-rate projects in the immediate submarket until post-occupancy visibility emerges.

stories.title: AI Infrastructure Firm Treeswift Signs 7K-SF Lease at 256 West 38th Street
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-driven infrastructure technology company is relocating its offices to Midtown. Philadelphia-based Treeswift signed a four-year, 7,487-square-foot lease on the entire 11th floor of the Hakimian Organization’s 256 West 38th Street in an expansion of its New York City operations, according to landlord broker Lee & Associates NYC. Asking rent was $39 per square foot. It is unclear where Treeswift is relocating from within New York City, but the company also has an office in Philadelphia. “Artificial intelligence companies have become one of the most active drivers of office leasing demand in Manhattan, but they are not all looking for trophy towers,” Lee & Associates’ Todd Korren, who represented the landlord alongside Noah Caspi, said in a statement. “As these businesses grow, they are seeking efficient, well-connected headquarters that support collaboration, attract talent and provide long-term value. Treeswift’s relocation reflects that trend.” Daniel Rodriguez Sains of Buchbinder Warren negotiated on behalf of the tenant and did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Treeswift specializes in helping clients with infrastructure inspections, vegetation management, construction planning, wildfire mitigation and storm response, according to the brokerage. The firm will move into its new offices at 256 West 38th Street in August. It’s unclear when the Rex Hakimian-led firm got involved in the building’s ownership, but his name starts showing up on deed filings sometime after March 2025, when Empire Capital Holdings acquired the property and nearby 229 West 36th Street in a state of distress for a steep discount at $50 million. The seller, Investcorp, purchased the two buildings for $157 million in 2017, Commercial Observer previously reported. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: TreeSwift (Philadelphia AI/infrastructure firm) signed 7.5K-SF lease at 256 West 38th, Midtown; $39/SF asking
Four-year lease on full 11th floor; expansion of NYC operations; no prior submarket disclosed

stories.summary: TreeSwift, a Philadelphia-based AI-driven infrastructure technology company, signed a four-year, 7,487-square-foot lease on the entire 11th floor of 256 West 38th Street in Midtown Manhattan at $39 per square foot, expanding its NYC operations. The company also maintains offices in Philadelphia. Landlord broker Lee & Associates noted that AI companies are increasingly seeking efficient, collaborative headquarters in secondary-tier office buildings rather than trophy towers.
stories.impact: AI firms' pivot to efficient, mid-market office in Midtown (not trophy towers) is driving selective demand in secondary office stock and compressing trophy office relevance—this capital and talent concentration in tier-2 office locations will support selective conversion economics and reduce the urgency for large format repositioning, while increasing residential demand pressure in Midtown corridors with easy transit access to tech employment clusters.

stories.title: PCCP, Stonemont Close on $1B-Plus Acquisition of Blackstone Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: PCCP and Stonemont Financial Group are officially the new owners of a 5.9 million-square-foot industrial portfolio, Commercial Observer can first report. The joint venture acquired the 38 assets, located across 14 markets in 10 states, for upward of $1 billion with Blackstone as the seller, according to an article from Real Estate Alert preceding the sale. The portfolio was sold via an off-market transaction, with Eastdil Secured serving as adviser, and the transaction closed July 29. It wasn’t immediately clear how the acquisition was financed. “The acquisition of this portfolio represents PCCP’s continued conviction in the industrial sector and in markets we have actively invested in within the last five years,” Ryan Dodge, a partner with PCCP, said. “We believe our industrial portfolio continues to exhibit strong momentum, with increased leasing demand in recent months. In our view, this portfolio is well positioned to benefit from those same market tailwinds.” The portfolio — leased to a diverse roster of more than 70 tenants — is located across infill submarkets, including Denver, Dallas, Atlanta, and Charlotte, N.C., as well as strong growth markets like San Diego, Reno, Nev., and El Paso, Texas. With PCCP and Stonemount Financial now in the driver’s seat, the JV’s plan is to focus on revenue growth via contractual rent increases and marking-to-market on leases that are being renewed, according to a release. “This transaction reflects our conviction in the long-term fundamentals of the industrial real estate sector,” said Zack Markwell, CEO and managing principal at Stonemont. “We are pleased to have once again partnered with PCCP and will continue to pursue attractive acquisition opportunities alongside our active development program.” The industrial sector is one of PCCP’s investment fortés, with the firm currently managing more than 68 million square feet of industrial assets over 52 markets. This acquisition brings its count to 262 industrial transactions.
bullets: PCCP, Stonemont acquired Blackstone industrial portfolio: 5.9M SF, 38 assets, 14 markets, 10 states for $1B+
Off-market transaction closed July 29; Eastdil Secured adviser; financing details unclear
PCCP cites strong leasing demand momentum and conviction in industrial markets actively invested in past 5 years
stories.summary: PCCP and Stonemont Financial Group closed the acquisition of a 5.9 million-square-foot, 38-asset industrial portfolio spanning 14 markets across 10 states from Blackstone for upward of $1 billion. The off-market transaction, advised by Eastdil Secured, closed July 29, with financing details undisclosed. PCCP cited strong recent leasing demand momentum and strategic positioning in markets the firm has actively invested in over the past five years.
stories.impact: Institutional capital (PCCP/Stonemont) aggressively consolidating Blackstone's portfolio signals confidence in industrial fundamentals and rent-growth runway, but the $1B+ acquisition also suggests cap rates remain elevated enough to justify large-format portfolio plays—a market signal that ground-up industrial development and land assembly should remain attractive on the margin, particularly in secondary logistics hubs, though the scale of this acquisition may absorb available deal flow and compress cap rates inward.
